$$f\big(x + f(x) + y\big) + f\big(x - f(x) - y\big) = f(x+y) + f(x-y)$$
for every $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}$.
answer: Fix an odd positive integer $d$, an integer $k$ and odd integers $\ell_0, \ell_1, \dots, \ell_{d-1}$; then $f(md + i) = 2kmd + \ell_i d$ ($m\in\mathbb Z$, $0\le i\le d-1$). These are exactly the solutions.

prompt:
Let $n$ be a fixed integer with $n \ge 2$. We say that two polynomials $P$ and $Q$ with real coefficients are *block-similar* if for each $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ the sequences
$$P(2015i),\ P(2015i - 1),\ \dots,\ P(2015i - 2014)\qquad\text{and}\qquad Q(2015i),\ Q(2015i - 1),\ \dots,\ Q(2015i - 2014)$$
are permutations of each other.

(a) Prove that there exist distinct block-similar polynomials of degree $n + 1$.

(b) Prove that there do not exist distinct block-similar polynomials of degree $n$.
answer: (a) $P(x)=T(x)=\prod_{i=0}^n(x-2015i)$ and $Q(x)=T(x-1)$. (b) Summation polynomials show $P-Q=\alpha\big(T(x)-T(x-1)\big)$ and $P+Q$ constant, reducing to $P$ block-similar to $-P$, which fails by a sign/size argument on the first block.

prompt:
In Lineland there are $n \ge 1$ towns, arranged along a road running from left to right. Each town has a *left bulldozer* (put to the left of the town and facing left) and a *right bulldozer* (put to the right of the town and facing right). The sizes of the $2n$ bulldozers are distinct. Every time when a right and a left bulldozer confront each other, the larger bulldozer pushes the smaller one off the road. On the other hand, the bulldozers are quite unprotected at their rears; so, if a bulldozer reaches the rear-end of another one, the first one pushes the second one off the road, regardless of their sizes.

Let $A$ and $B$ be two towns, with $B$ being to the right of $A$. We say that town $A$ can *sweep town $B$ away* if the right bulldozer of $A$ can move over to $B$ pushing off all bulldozers it meets. Similarly, $B$ can sweep $A$ away if the left bulldozer of $B$ can move to $A$ pushing off all bulldozers of all towns on its way.

Prove that there is exactly one town which cannot be swept away by any other one.
answer: Induct on $n$: the largest useful bulldozer, say the right bulldozer of $T_k$, sweeps away every town to its right, and those towns cannot sweep anything at or left of $T_k$; delete them and apply induction to $T_1,\dots,T_k$.

prompt: For a finite set $A$ of positive integers, we call a partition of $A$ into two disjoint nonempty subsets $A_1$ and $A_2$ *good* if the least common multiple of the elements in $A_1$ is equal to the greatest common divisor of the elements in $A_2$. Determine the minimum value of $n$ such that there exists a set of $n$ positive integers with exactly $2015$ good partitions.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Two players $A$ and $B$ play a game in which they take turns choosing positive integers $k \le n$. The rules of the game are:

(i) A player cannot choose a number that has been chosen by either player on any previous turn.

(ii) A player cannot choose a number consecutive to any of those the player has already chosen on any previous turn.

(iii) The game is a draw if all numbers have been chosen; otherwise the player who cannot choose a number anymore loses the game.

The player $A$ takes the first turn. Determine the outcome of the game, assuming that both players use optimal strategies.
answer: The game is a draw for $n = 1, 2, 4, 6$; for all other $n$, player $B$ wins.

prompt: Let $S$ be a nonempty set of positive integers. We say that a positive integer $n$ is *clean* if it has a unique representation as a sum of an odd number of distinct elements from $S$. Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers that are not clean.
answer: Assume all $n>N$ are clean. Then representations are unique, every large number also has a unique *even* representation, and the even representation of any large $t\in S$ contains every element of $S$ between $N$ and $t$; this forces a gap $s_{p+1}\ge 2s_p$, and the even representation of $2s_p$ yields a second odd representation of $s_p$.

prompt: In a company of people some pairs are enemies. A group of people is called *unsociable* if the number of members in the group is odd and at least $3$, and it is possible to arrange all its members around a round table so that every two neighbors are enemies. Given that there are at most $2015$ unsociable groups, prove that it is possible to partition the company into $11$ parts so that no two enemies are in the same part.
answer: A graph with chromatic number $k\ge3$ has at least $2^{k-1}-k$ odd cycles with different vertex sets: in a lexicographically minimal $k$-colouring, for each odd set $C$ of at least $3$ colours there is an odd cycle using exactly the colours in $C$. Since $2^{11}-12>2015$, the chromatic number is at most $11$.

prompt: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with orthocenter $H$. Let $G$ be the point such that the quadrilateral $ABGH$ is a parallelogram. Let $I$ be the point on the line $GH$ such that $AC$ bisects $HI$. Suppose that the line $AC$ intersects the circumcircle of the triangle $GCI$ at $C$ and $J$. Prove that $IJ = AH$.
answer: $BGCH$ is cyclic (right angles at $B$ and $H$), so $\angle CJI=\angle CGH=\angle CBH=\angle HAC$; with $M=AC\cap GH$ the midpoint of $HI$ and $D$ the reflection of $A$ across the foot of the perpendicular from $H$ to $AC$, triangles $IMJ$ and $HMD$ are congruent, so $IJ=HD=AH$.

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle C = 90^\circ$, and let $H$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$. A point $D$ is chosen inside the triangle $CBH$ so that $CH$ bisects $AD$. Let $P$ be the intersection point of the lines $BD$ and $CH$. Let $\omega$ be the semicircle with diameter $BD$ that meets the segment $CB$ at an interior point. A line through $P$ is tangent to $\omega$ at $Q$. Prove that the lines $CQ$ and $AD$ meet on $\omega$.
answer: With $K$, $L$ the projections of $D$ on $AB$ and of $Q$ on $DB$: $\frac{AH}{HB}=\frac{PD}{PB}=\frac{DL}{LB}$ (parallel lines and the bisector theorem, $QD$ bisecting $\angle PQL$), so the spiral similarity at $B$ taking $A\mapsto D$ takes $H\mapsto L$ and $C\mapsto Q$; then $\angle ADB=\angle CQB$ and the intersection of $AD$, $CQ$ lies on the circle $BDQ$.

prompt: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $AC$. A circle $\omega$ passing through $B$ and $M$ meets the sides $AB$ and $BC$ again at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $T$ be the point such that the quadrilateral $BPTQ$ is a parallelogram. Suppose that $T$ lies on the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$. Determine all possible values of $BT/BM$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $CA \ne CB$. Let $D$, $F$, and $G$ be the midpoints of the sides $AB$, $AC$, and $BC$, respectively. A circle $\Gamma$ passing through $C$ and tangent to $AB$ at $D$ meets the segments $AF$ and $BG$ at $H$ and $I$, respectively. The points $H'$ and $I'$ are symmetric to $H$ and $I$ about $F$ and $G$, respectively. The line $H'I'$ meets $CD$ and $FG$ at $Q$ and $M$, respectively. The line $CM$ meets $\Gamma$ again at $P$. Prove that $CQ = QP$.
answer: With $R$, $S$ the second intersections of $DF$, $DG$ with $\Gamma$: powers of points show $H'I'GF$, $ADH'R$, $RSGF$ cyclic, so $R,S$ lie on $H'I'$ and $C,P,I',H'$ are concyclic; then $QH'\cdot QR=QC^2=QI'\cdot QS$, and the inversion at $Q$ with radius $QC$ swaps $\Gamma$ and the circle $CH'I'$, fixing $P$, so $QP=QC$.

prompt: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral, and let $P$, $Q$, $R$, and $S$ be points on the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Let the line segments $PR$ and $QS$ meet at $O$. Suppose that each of the quadrilaterals $APOS$, $BQOP$, $CROQ$, and $DSOR$ has an incircle. Prove that the lines $AC$, $PQ$, and $RS$ are either concurrent or parallel to each other.
answer: By Menelaus it suffices to show $\frac{AP}{PB}\cdot\frac{BQ}{QC}\cdot\frac{CR}{RD}\cdot\frac{DS}{SA}=1$; this follows from the incenter identity $\frac{EF\cdot FG}{GH\cdot HE}=\frac{FM^2}{HM^2}$ for a tangential quadrilateral $EFGH$ with incenter $M$, applied to the four small quadrilaterals, together with similar right triangles formed by neighbouring incenters.

prompt:
A *triangulation* of a convex polygon $\Pi$ is a partitioning of $\Pi$ into triangles by diagonals having no common points other than the vertices of the polygon. We say that a triangulation is a *Thaiangulation* if all triangles in it have the same area.

Prove that any two different Thaiangulations of a convex polygon $\Pi$ differ by exactly two triangles. (In other words, prove that it is possible to replace one pair of triangles in the first Thaiangulation with a different pair of triangles so as to obtain the second Thaiangulation.)
answer: Key facts: a triangulation contains at most one parallelogram (two triangles forming a parallelogram), and every triangle of a Thaiangulation has a side on $\Pi$ (affine map to an equilateral triangle). Then a minimal counterexample, examined at an ear of one Thaiangulation, produces a triangulation with two parallelograms.

prompt: Determine all positive integers $M$ for which the sequence $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$, defined by $a_0 = \dfrac{2M+1}{2}$ and $a_{k+1} = a_k\lfloor a_k\rfloor$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, contains at least one integer term.
answer: All integers $M \ge 2$ (for $M = 1$ the sequence is constantly $\frac32$).

prompt: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers such that $a!\,b!$ is a multiple of $a! + b!$. Prove that $3a \ge 2b + 2$.
answer: For $a<b$ write $c=b-a$ and $M=\frac{b!}{a!}$; then $1+M \mid a!$, and coprimality with $c!$ (and with $c+1$ when $a=2c+1$) gives $1+M \mid (c+1)(c+2)\cdots a$. If $a\le 2c+1$, the right side is smaller than $M$, a contradiction; so $a\ge 2c+2$.

prompt: Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers such that $m > n$. Define $x_k = \dfrac{m+k}{n+k}$ for $k = 1, 2, \dots, n+1$. Prove that if all the numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{n+1}$ are integers, then $x_1x_2\cdots x_{n+1} - 1$ is divisible by an odd prime.
answer: With $a_k = x_k - 1 = \frac{m-n}{n+k}$: exactly one of $n+1,\dots,2n+1$ (namely $2^c$) has the maximal power of $2$. So all $a_k$ but one are divisible by $2^{d-c+1}$ while $P = \prod(a_k+1)-1 \equiv a_\ell \not\equiv 0$, yet $P \ge 2^{d-c+1}$; hence $P$ is not a power of $2$.

prompt:
Suppose that $a_0, a_1, \dots$ and $b_0, b_1, \dots$ are two sequences of positive integers satisfying $a_0, b_0 \ge 2$ and
$$a_{n+1} = \gcd(a_n, b_n) + 1,\qquad b_{n+1} = \operatorname{lcm}(a_n, b_n) - 1$$
for all $n \ge 0$. Prove that the sequence $(a_n)$ is eventually periodic; in other words, there exist integers $N \ge 0$ and $t > 0$ such that $a_{n+t} = a_n$ for all $n \ge N$.
answer: With $s_n = a_n + b_n$ and $w_n$ the least $m \ge a_n$ not dividing $s_n$, the sequence $(w_n)$ is non-increasing, hence eventually constant $= w$, and $g_n = \gcd(w, s_n)$ is then constant $= g$; so $(a_n)$ eventually cycles through $g+1, g+2, \dots, w$.

prompt:
Let $\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ denote the set of positive integers. Consider a function $f:\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\to\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$. For any $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ we write $f^n(m) = \underbrace{f(f(\dots f}_{n}(m)\dots))$. Suppose that $f$ has the following two properties:

(i) If $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, then $\dfrac{f^n(m) - m}{n} \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$;

(ii) The set $\mathbb{Z}_{>0} \setminus \{f(n) \mid n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}\}$ is finite.

Prove that the sequence $f(1) - 1,\ f(2) - 2,\ f(3) - 3,\ \dots$ is periodic.
answer: $f$ is injective with $f(m)>m$, so the positive integers split into finitely many chains $a_i, f(a_i), f^2(a_i),\dots$. A density/pigeonhole argument plus divisibility by $y-j$ shows every chain is an arithmetic progression (step $T_i$), and then $f(n+T)-(n+T)=f(n)-n$ with $T=\operatorname{lcm}(T_i)$.

prompt: Let $\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ denote the set of positive integers. For any positive integer $k$, a function $f:\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\to\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is called *$k$-good* if $\gcd\big(f(m) + n, f(n) + m\big) \le k$ for all $m \ne n$. Find all $k$ such that there exists a $k$-good function.
answer: Exactly the $k \ge 2$. No $1$-good function exists (a parity argument), and $f(n) = 2^{g(n)+1} - n - 1$ with $g(1) = 1$, $g(n+1) = \big(2^{g(n)+1}\big)!$ is $2$-good.

prompt:
For every positive integer $n$ with prime factorization $n = \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i^{\alpha_i}$, define
$$\mho(n) = \sum_{i:\ p_i > 10^{100}} \alpha_i .$$
That is, $\mho(n)$ is the number of prime factors of $n$ greater than $10^{100}$, counted with multiplicity.

Find all strictly increasing functions $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ such that
$$\mho\big(f(a) - f(b)\big) \le \mho(a - b)\quad\text{for all integers } a \text{ and } b \text{ with } a > b.$$
answer: $f(x) = ax + b$, where $b$ is any integer and $a$ is a positive integer with $\mho(a) = 0$ (no prime factor above $10^{100}$).

prompt:
Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be positive real numbers such that $\min\{ab,bc,ca\}\ge 1$. Prove that
$$\sqrt[3]{(a^2+1)(b^2+1)(c^2+1)}\le\left(\frac{a+b+c}{3}\right)^2+1.$$
answer: Key lemma: if $xy\ge1$ then $(x^2+1)(y^2+1)\le\big((\tfrac{x+y}2)^2+1\big)^2$. With $a\ge b\ge c$ and $d=\frac{a+b+c}3$ apply it to $(a,d)$, $(b,c)$ and then to $(\frac{a+d}2,\frac{b+c}2)$ to get $(a^2+1)(b^2+1)(c^2+1)(d^2+1)\le(d^2+1)^4$.

prompt:
Find the smallest real constant $C$ such that for any positive real numbers $a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4$ and $a_5$ (not necessarily distinct), one can always choose distinct subscripts $i,j,k$ and $l$ such that
$$\left|\frac{a_i}{a_j}-\frac{a_k}{a_l}\right|\le C.$$

Find all integers $n\ge3$ with the following property: for all real numbers $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ and $b_1,b_2,\dots,b_n$ satisfying $|a_k|+|b_k|=1$ for $1\le k\le n$, there exist $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$, each of which is either $-1$ or $1$, such that
$$\left|\sum_{k=1}^n x_ka_k\right|+\left|\sum_{k=1}^n x_kb_k\right|\le1.$$
answer: Exactly the odd $n\ge3$. For even $n$ the example $a_k=0,b_k=1$ ($k<n$), $a_n=1,b_n=0$ fails by parity; for odd $n$ make all $b_k\ge0$, sort the $a_k$ decreasingly and take alternating signs $x_k=(-1)^{k+1}$.

prompt:
Denote by $\mathbb R^+$ the set of all positive real numbers. Find all functions $f:\mathbb R^+\to\mathbb R^+$ such that
$$xf(x^2)f(f(y))+f(yf(x))=f(xy)\Big(f\big(f(x^2)\big)+f\big(f(y^2)\big)\Big)$$
for all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$.

(a) Prove that for every positive integer $n$, there exists a fraction $\frac ab$ where $a$ and $b$ are integers satisfying $0<b\le\sqrt n+1$ and $\sqrt n\le\frac ab\le\sqrt{n+1}$.

(b) Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that there is no fraction $\frac ab$ where $a$ and $b$ are integers satisfying $0<b\le\sqrt n$ and $\sqrt n\le\frac ab\le\sqrt{n+1}$.
answer: (a) Write $n=r^2+s$ with $0\le s\le2r$; use $r+\frac{s}{2r}$ (denominator $r$) if $s$ is even and $(r+1)-\frac{2r+1-s}{2(r+1)}$ (denominator $r+1$) if $s$ is odd. (b) $n=r^2+1$ works: $a^2$ would lie strictly between $(br)^2$ and $(br+1)^2$.

prompt:
Denote by $\mathbb R$ the set of all real numbers. Find all functions $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that $f(0)\ne0$ and
$$f(x+y)^2=2f(x)f(y)+\max\big\{f(x^2)+f(y^2),\ f(x^2+y^2)\big\}$$
for all real numbers $x$ and $y$.
answer: $f(x)=-1$ for all $x$, and $f(x)=x-1$ for all $x$ (show $f(0)=-1$ and $f(x)+f(-x)=-2$; then $g=f+1$ is additive with $g(x^2)=g(x)^2$).

prompt:
Determine the largest real number $a$ such that for all $n\ge1$ and for all real numbers $x_0,x_1,\dots,x_n$ satisfying $0=x_0<x_1<x_2<\dots<x_n$, we have
$$\frac1{x_1-x_0}+\frac1{x_2-x_1}+\dots+\frac1{x_n-x_{n-1}}\ge a\left(\frac2{x_1}+\frac3{x_2}+\dots+\frac{n+1}{x_n}\right).$$

The leader of an IMO team chooses positive integers $n$ and $k$ with $n>k$, and announces them to the deputy leader and a contestant. The leader then secretly tells the deputy leader an $n$-digit binary string, and the deputy leader writes down all $n$-digit binary strings which differ from the leader's in exactly $k$ positions. (For example, if $n=3$ and $k=1$, and if the leader chooses $101$, the deputy leader would write down $001$, $111$ and $100$.) The contestant is allowed to look at the strings written by the deputy leader and guess the leader's string. What is the minimum number of guesses (in terms of $n$ and $k$) needed to guarantee the correct answer?
answer: $2$ guesses if $n=2k$, and $1$ guess if $n\ne2k$ (count, for each position, how many written strings have a $0$ or a $1$ there).

prompt:
Find all positive integers $n$ for which all positive divisors of $n$ can be put into the cells of a rectangular table under the following constraints:

- each cell contains a distinct divisor;
- the sums of all rows are equal; and
- the sums of all columns are equal.

Let $n$ be a positive integer relatively prime to $6$. We paint the vertices of a regular $n$-gon with three colours so that there is an odd number of vertices of each colour. Show that there exists an isosceles triangle whose three vertices are of different colours.
answer: Double count pairs (isosceles triangle, side with two colours). If no triangle is three-coloured, the count is even. But each two-coloured pair of vertices lies in exactly $3$ isosceles triangles, so the count is $3(bc+cd+db)$, which is odd.

prompt: Let $n\ge3$ be a positive integer. Find the maximum number of diagonals of a regular $n$-gon one can select, so that any two of them do not intersect in the interior or they are perpendicular to each other.
answer: $n-2$ if $n$ is even and $n-3$ if $n$ is odd (for odd $n$ no two diagonals are perpendicular; for even $n$ induct over cyclic polygons, and use all diagonals from one vertex $A$ plus the diagonal joining the two neighbours of the vertex opposite $A$).

prompt:
There are $n\ge3$ islands in a city. Initially, the ferry company offers some routes between some pairs of islands so that it is impossible to divide the islands into two groups such that no two islands in different groups are connected by a ferry route.

After each year, the ferry company will close a ferry route between some two islands $X$ and $Y$. At the same time, in order to maintain its service, the company will open new routes according to the following rule: for any island which is connected by a ferry route to exactly one of $X$ and $Y$, a new route between this island and the other of $X$ and $Y$ is added.

Suppose at any moment, if we partition all islands into two nonempty groups in any way, then it is known that the ferry company will close a certain route connecting two islands from the two groups after some years. Prove that after some years there will be an island which is connected to all other islands by ferry routes.
answer: Maintain two disjoint sets $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ that form a "network" (every island of $\mathcal A$ is joined to every island of $\mathcal B$). A closed $\mathcal A$–$\mathcal B$ route $AB$ gives the new network $\{A,B\}$ versus the rest, and a closed route from the network to an outside island $D$ lets $D$ join. Once the network covers all islands, the next two closures produce an island joined to everyone.

prompt: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Determine the smallest positive integer $k$ with the following property: it is possible to mark $k$ cells on a $2n\times2n$ board so that there exists a unique partition of the board into $1\times2$ and $2\times1$ dominoes, none of which contains two marked cells.

In a convex pentagon $ABCDE$, let $F$ be a point on $AC$ such that $\angle FBC=90^\circ$. Suppose triangles $ABF$, $ACD$ and $ADE$ are similar isosceles triangles with
$$\angle FAB=\angle FBA=\angle DAC=\angle DCA=\angle EAD=\angle EDA.$$
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $CF$. Point $X$ is chosen such that $AMXE$ is a parallelogram. Show that $BD$, $EM$ and $FX$ are concurrent.
answer: $F$ lies on the circle with centre $E$ through $A$ and $D$; $B,F,E$ and $E,D,X$ are collinear; $\triangle EFA\cong\triangle MFB$ gives $\triangle EMB\cong\triangle EMX$, so $BD$ and $XF$ are mirror images in $EM$ and meet on it. (This is IMO 2016 Problem 1, stated differently there.)

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcircle $\Gamma$ and incentre $I$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. Denote by $D$ the foot of perpendicular from $I$ to side $BC$. The line through $I$ perpendicular to $AI$ meets sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $F$ and $E$ respectively. Suppose the circumcircle of triangle $AEF$ intersects $\Gamma$ at a point $X$ other than $A$. Prove that lines $XD$ and $AM$ meet on $\Gamma$.
answer: Let $AM$ meet $\Gamma$ again at $Y$ and $XY$ meet $BC$ at $D'$. The chord-ratio lemma gives $\frac{BD'}{D'C}=\frac{XB}{XC}\cdot\frac{AC}{AB}$; the spiral similarity $XBF\sim XCE$ gives $\frac{XB}{XC}=\frac{BF}{CE}=\big(\frac{\sin(C/2)}{\sin(B/2)}\big)^2$; together $\frac{BD'}{D'C}=\frac{\tan(C/2)}{\tan(B/2)}=\frac{BD}{DC}$.

prompt:
Let $B=(-1,0)$ and $C=(1,0)$ be fixed points on the coordinate plane. A nonempty, bounded subset $S$ of the plane is said to be *nice* if

(i) there is a point $T$ in $S$ such that for every point $Q$ in $S$, the segment $TQ$ lies entirely in $S$; and

(ii) for any triangle $P_1P_2P_3$, there exists a unique point $A$ in $S$ and a permutation $\sigma$ of the indices $\{1,2,3\}$ for which triangles $ABC$ and $P_{\sigma(1)}P_{\sigma(2)}P_{\sigma(3)}$ are similar.

Prove that there exist two distinct nice subsets $S$ and $S'$ of the set $\{(x,y):x\ge0,\ y\ge0\}$ such that if $A\in S$ and $A'\in S'$ are the unique choices of points in (ii), then the product $BA\cdot BA'$ is a constant independent of the triangle $P_1P_2P_3$.
answer: Take $S=\{x,y\ge0,\ (x+1)^2+y^2\le4\}$ (where $BC$ is the longest side and $AB\ge AC$) and $S'=\{x,y\ge0,\ (x+1)^2+y^2\ge4,\ (x-1)^2+y^2\le4\}$ (where $BC$ is the middle side), star-shaped from $(1,2)$. If the sides are $p\ge q\ge r$, then $BA=\frac{2q}{p}$ and $BA'=\frac{2p}{q}$, so $BA\cdot BA'=4$.

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB=AC\ne BC$ and let $I$ be its incentre. The line $BI$ meets $AC$ at $D$, and the line through $D$ perpendicular to $AC$ meets $AI$ at $E$. Prove that the reflection of $I$ in $AC$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $BDE$.
answer: With $I'$ the reflection, $DE$ is the external bisector of $\angle BDI'$, so it suffices to show $EB=EI'$. With $T,M$ the touch points of the incircle on $AB,BC$: $DT=DM$, and the similar triangles $DAT\sim EAI'$ and $DAM\sim EAB$ give $EI'=DT\cdot\frac{AI}{AT}$ and $EB=DM\cdot\frac{AB}{AM}$, where $\frac{AI}{AT}=\frac{AB}{AM}$.

prompt: Let $D$ be the foot of perpendicular from $A$ to the Euler line (the line passing through the circumcentre and the orthocentre) of an acute scalene triangle $ABC$. A circle $\omega$ with centre $S$ passes through $A$ and $D$, and it intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $X$ and $Y$ respectively. Let $P$ be the foot of altitude from $A$ to $BC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Prove that the circumcentre of triangle $XSY$ is equidistant from $P$ and $M$.
answer: As $S$ moves on the perpendicular bisector of $AD$, the spiral similarity about $D$ carrying one configuration $(S,X,Y)$ to another shows that the circumcentre $O_1$ of $XSY$ is the image of $S$ under a fixed similarity, so $O_1$ moves on a line. For $S$ the midpoint of $AH$ (giving the nine-point centre) and for $S$ the midpoint of $AO$ (giving a point on the perpendicular bisector of the midline), $O_1$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $PM$; so that line is the whole locus.

prompt: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $\angle ABC=\angle ADC<90^\circ$. The internal angle bisectors of $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ADC$ meet $AC$ at $E$ and $F$ respectively, and meet each other at point $P$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AC$ and let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $BPD$. Segments $BM$ and $DM$ intersect $\omega$ again at $X$ and $Y$ respectively. Denote by $Q$ the intersection point of lines $XE$ and $YF$. Prove that $PQ\perp AC$.
answer: $Y$ lies on circle $ABC$ and $MY\cdot MD=MA^2$, so $YF$ bisects $\angle AYC$ and $YB'$ (with $B'$ the arc midpoint) is the external bisector. The line through $P$ parallel to $AC$ meets $\omega$ again at a point $S$ on $YB'$, and similarly on the external bisector at $X$. Hence $\angle QYS=\angle QXS=90^\circ$, $QS$ is a diameter of $\omega$, and $PQ\perp PS\parallel AC$.

prompt:
Let $I$ be the incentre of a non-equilateral triangle $ABC$, $I_A$ be the $A$-excentre, $I'_A$ be the reflection of $I_A$ in $BC$, and $l_A$ be the reflection of line $AI'_A$ in $AI$. Define points $I_B$, $I'_B$ and line $l_B$ analogously. Let $P$ be the intersection point of $l_A$ and $l_B$.

(a) Prove that $P$ lies on line $OI$ where $O$ is the circumcentre of triangle $ABC$.

(b) Let one of the tangents from $P$ to the incircle of triangle $ABC$ meet the circumcircle at points $X$ and $Y$. Show that $\angle XIY=120^\circ$.
answer: (a) $P$ is the inverse $P^*$ of $I$ in the circumcircle: $P^*$ lies on ray $OI$ with $OP^*=\frac{R^2}{OI}$. Power of a point gives $A,M,O,P^*$ concyclic ($M$ the arc midpoint), and an angle chase via $\triangle AA'I_A\sim\triangle AIO$ ($A'$ the reflection of $A$ in $BC$) puts $P^*$ on $l_A$; likewise on $l_B$. answer: Proof: the images $f^m(S)$ stabilise, so $f$ permutes the final image and $f^{m+r}=f^m$ for large $m$; choose $n\ge3$ with $f^{n+2}=f^{2n+1}$. Then $g=f^n$ satisfies $f\circ g\circ f=g\circ f\circ g$, so $f^n=f$, which gives $f(T)=T$.

Prove that Sisyphus cannot reach the aim in less than
$$\left\lceil\frac n1\right\rceil+\left\lceil\frac n2\right\rceil+\left\lceil\frac n3\right\rceil+\dots+\left\lceil\frac nn\right\rceil$$
turns. (As usual, $\lceil x\rceil$ stands for the least integer not smaller than $x$.)
answer: Proof: number the stones $1,\dots,n$ and always move the highest-numbered stone of the chosen square. Then stone $k$ is only moved from squares with at most $k$ stones, so it moves at most $k$ squares per turn and needs at least $\lceil n/k\rceil$ turns.

prompt: Let $k$ be a positive integer. The organising committee of a tennis tournament is to schedule the matches for $2k$ players so that every two players play once, each day exactly one match is played, and each player arrives to the tournament site the day of his first match, and departs the day of his last match. For every day a player is present on the tournament, the committee has to pay $1$ coin to the hotel. The organisers want to design the schedule so as to minimise the total cost of all players' stays. Determine this minimum cost.
answer: $\dfrac{k(4k^2+k-1)}2$ coins (bound each sorted stay $e_{i+1}-b_{i+1}+1$ by counting matches that can happen before the $(i+1)$-th arrival and after the $(i+1)$-th-last departure; a two-group schedule attains all bounds).

prompt:
Let $a$ and $b$ be distinct positive integers. The following infinite process takes place on an initially empty board.

(i) If there is at least a pair of equal numbers on the board, we choose such a pair and increase one of its components by $a$ and the other by $b$.

(ii) If no such pair exists, we write down two times the number $0$.

Prove that, no matter how we make the choices in (i), operation (ii) will be performed only finitely many times.
answer: Proof: let $f(k)$ count how many times $k$ has appeared when (ii) is about to be applied for the $(N+1)$-th time; then $f(k)=\lfloor f(k-a)/2\rfloor+\lfloor f(k-b)/2\rfloor$ for $k\ge1$, so $f(sa+tb)>f(0)/2^{s+t}-2$; for large $N$ this forces $f\ge2$ on all integers beyond $ab-a-b$, i.e. infinitely many numbers, impossible.

prompt: Consider $2018$ pairwise crossing circles no three of which are concurrent. These circles subdivide the plane into regions bounded by circular *edges* that meet at *vertices*. Notice that there are an even number of vertices on each circle. Given the circle, alternately colour the vertices on that circle red and blue. In doing so for each circle, every vertex is coloured twice — once for each of the two circles that cross at that point. If the two colourings agree at a vertex, then it is assigned that colour; otherwise, it becomes yellow. Show that, if some circle contains at least $2061$ yellow points, then the vertices of some region are all yellow.
answer: Proof: if a circle has $k$ yellow points, parity lemmas (two crossing points of a pair of circles are both yellow or both not; every "triangle" of arcs has an odd number of yellow corners) force at least $\frac{k^2}2-(n-2)k+(n-1)(n-2)$ yellow vertices. If every region had a non-yellow vertex, each region would have at least two (non-yellow vertices alternate in colour around a region), giving at most $\frac{n(n-1)}2-1$ yellow vertices. Together $k\le n-2+\lfloor\sqrt{n-2}\rfloor=2060$.

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB=AC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $P$ be a point such that $PB<PC$ and $PA$ is parallel to $BC$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on the lines $PB$ and $PC$, respectively, so that $B$ lies on the segment $PX$, $C$ lies on the segment $PY$, and $\angle PXM=\angle PYM$. Prove that the quadrilateral $APXY$ is cyclic.
answer: Proof: let $Z$ be the point of line $AM$ with $ZY\perp PC$. Then $P,A,Y,Z$ lie on the circle with diameter $PZ$; $CYZM$ is cyclic, so $\angle CZM=\angle CYM=\angle BXM$, and by symmetry $\angle BZM=\angle CZM$, so $B,X,Z,M$ are concyclic and $\angle PXZ=90^\circ$. Hence $X$ is on that circle too.

prompt:
A circle $\omega$ of radius $1$ is given. A collection $T$ of triangles is called *good*, if the following conditions hold:

(i) each triangle from $T$ is inscribed in $\omega$;

(ii) no two triangles from $T$ have a common interior point.

Determine all positive real numbers $t$ such that, for each positive integer $n$, there exists a good collection of $n$ triangles, each of perimeter greater than $t$.
answer: Exactly $0<t\le4$ (fan triangles from one end of a diameter all have perimeter $>4$; if $t=4+2\varepsilon$, Heron's formula gives each triangle area $\ge\sqrt{(2+\varepsilon)\varepsilon^3}$, so only boundedly many fit in the disc).

prompt: A point $T$ is chosen inside a triangle $ABC$. Let $A_1$, $B_1$, and $C_1$ be the reflections of $T$ in $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of the triangle $A_1B_1C_1$. The lines $A_1T$, $B_1T$, and $C_1T$ meet $\Omega$ again at $A_2$, $B_2$, and $C_2$, respectively. Prove that the lines $AA_2$, $BB_2$, and $CC_2$ are concurrent on $\Omega$.
answer: Proof (directed angles): $C$ is the circumcentre of $A_1TB_1$, which gives $\measuredangle(CA_1,CB)=\measuredangle(C_2A_1,C_2B_2)$ and similarly at $B$; so $A_1BC\sim A_1B_2C_2$, hence $A_1BB_2\sim A_1CC_2$, and the second intersection $K$ of $CC_2$ with $\Omega$ lies on $BB_2$ (and likewise on $AA_2$).

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcircle $\omega$ and incentre $I$. A line $\ell$ intersects the lines $AI$, $BI$, and $CI$ at points $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively, distinct from the points $A$, $B$, $C$, and $I$. The perpendicular bisectors $x$, $y$, and $z$ of the segments $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$, respectively determine a triangle $\Theta$. Show that the circumcircle of the triangle $\Theta$ is tangent to $\omega$.
answer: Proof: $\Theta=XYZ$ is homothetic to $X_0Y_0Z_0$, where $X_0,Y_0,Z_0$ are the midpoints of arcs ($Y_0Z_0$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AI$, parallel to $x$). The reflections of $\ell$ in $x,y,z$ concur at a point $T\in\omega$, and an angle chase shows $T\in XX_0$, $YY_0$, $ZZ_0$; so $T$ is the centre of the homothety, which then maps $\omega$ to the circle $XYZ$ and fixes $T\in\omega$, giving tangency at $T$.

prompt: Let $O$ be the circumcentre, and $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. Let $P$ be an arbitrary point on $\Omega$, distinct from $A$, $B$, $C$, and their antipodes in $\Omega$. Denote the circumcentres of the triangles $AOP$, $BOP$, and $COP$ by $O_A$, $O_B$, and $O_C$, respectively. The lines $\ell_A$, $\ell_B$, and $\ell_C$ perpendicular to $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ pass through $O_A$, $O_B$, and $O_C$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle formed by $\ell_A$, $\ell_B$, and $\ell_C$ is tangent to the line $OP$.
answer: Proof (directed angles): with $L_A=\ell_B\cap\ell_C$ etc., the points $L_B,P,O_A,O_C$ are concyclic (and similarly), which shows $P$ lies on the circle $L_AL_BL_C$ and that $P,L_C,C$ (and $P,L_A,A$) are collinear; then $\measuredangle(OP,PL_A)=\measuredangle(PA,AO)=\measuredangle(PL_C,L_CL_A)$, the tangent–chord condition.

prompt: Determine all pairs $(n,k)$ of distinct positive integers such that there exists a positive integer $s$ for which the numbers of divisors of $sn$ and of $sk$ are equal.
answer: Exactly the pairs with $n\nmid k$ and $k\nmid n$ (if $n\mid k$, the divisors of $sn$ form a proper subset of those of $sk$; otherwise choose the exponents of $s$ so that the ratios $\frac{\alpha_i+\gamma_i+1}{\beta_i+\gamma_i+1}$ telescope to $1$).

prompt:
Let $n>1$ be a positive integer. Each cell of an $n\times n$ table contains an integer. Suppose that the following conditions are satisfied:

(i) Each number in the table is congruent to $1$ modulo $n$;

(ii) The sum of numbers in any row, as well as the sum of numbers in any column, is congruent to $n$ modulo $n^2$.

Let $R_i$ be the product of the numbers in the $i^{\text{th}}$ row, and $C_j$ be the product of the numbers in the $j^{\text{th}}$ column. Prove that the sums $R_1+\dots+R_n$ and $C_1+\dots+C_n$ are congruent modulo $n^4$.
answer: Proof: with $P$ the product of all entries, show $\sum R_i\equiv n-1+P\pmod{n^4}$ (and the same for columns): each $R_i\equiv1\pmod{n^2}$, so $P=\prod R_i\equiv1+\sum(R_i-1)\pmod{n^4}$.

prompt: Define the sequence $a_0,a_1,a_2,\dots$ by $a_n=2^n+2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$. Prove that there are infinitely many terms of the sequence which can be expressed as a sum of (two or more) distinct terms of the sequence, as well as infinitely many of those which cannot be expressed in such a way.
answer: Proof: with $S_{n-1}=a_0+\dots+a_{n-1}=2^n+2^{\lceil n/2\rceil}+2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}-3$, complements show $a_n$ is such a sum iff $2^{\lceil n/2\rceil}-3$ is a sum of distinct terms, and that $2^t-3$ and $2^{4t-6}-3$ behave alike. Starting from $2^3-3=a_0+a_1$ (yes) and $2^7-3=125$ (no) gives infinitely many of each.

prompt:
Four positive integers $x$, $y$, $z$, and $t$ satisfy the relations
$$xy-zt=x+y=z+t.$$
Is it possible that both $xy$ and $zt$ are perfect squares?

Let $f:\{1,2,3,\dots\}\to\{2,3,\dots\}$ be a function such that $f(m+n)\mid f(m)+f(n)$ for all pairs $m,n$ of positive integers. Prove that there exists a positive integer $c>1$ which divides all values of $f$.
answer: Proof: if $S_m=\{n:m\mid f(n)\}$ is infinite then it is the set of multiples of $\min S_m$. If $f$ is bounded, only finitely many primes occur; a prime dividing $f(N d_1\cdots d_k+1)$ for large $N$ then divides every value. If $f$ is unbounded, "peaks" $p$ satisfy $f(k)+f(p-k)=f(p)$, and peaks with equal $f$ mod $a=f(1)$ show $S_a$ is infinite, so $f(1)$ divides all values.

prompt:
Let $n\ge2018$ be an integer, and let $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n,b_1,b_2,\dots,b_n$ be pairwise distinct positive integers not exceeding $5n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$\frac{a_1}{b_1},\ \frac{a_2}{b_2},\ \dots,\ \frac{a_n}{b_n}$$
forms an arithmetic progression. Prove that the terms of the sequence are equal.
answer:
Proof: if the common difference is $c/d
e0$ in lowest terms, then for each prime $p\mid d$ the indices $i$ with $
u_p(b_i)<
u_p(d)$ lie in one residue class mod $p$. This forces $d$ to have only prime factors $2,3,5$, and then $d\mid b_i$ for at least $8$ indices in every block of $30$. Since at least $n/2$ terms lie in $(0,10]$, $d> rac{n-2}{20}$, and these multiples of $d$ would exceed $5n$.

prompt:
Let $u_1,u_2,\dots,u_{2019}$ be real numbers satisfying
$$u_1+u_2+\dots+u_{2019}=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad u_1^2+u_2^2+\dots+u_{2019}^2=1.$$
Let $a=\min(u_1,u_2,\dots,u_{2019})$ and $b=\max(u_1,u_2,\dots,u_{2019})$. Prove that
$$ab\le-\frac1{2019}.$$
answer: Proof: split the indices into positive ($p$ of them) and nonpositive ($n$ of them) terms; $\sum_P u_i^2\le b\sum_P u_i=b\sum_N|u_i|\le -nab$ and $\sum_N u_i^2\le -pab$, so $1\le-2019ab$.

prompt:
Let $n\ge3$ be a positive integer and let $(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n)$ be a strictly increasing sequence of $n$ positive real numbers with sum equal to $2$. Let $X$ be a subset of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ such that the value of
$$\Big|1-\sum_{i\in X}a_i\Big|$$
is minimised. Prove that there exists a strictly increasing sequence of $n$ positive real numbers $(b_1,b_2,\dots,b_n)$ with sum equal to $2$ such that
$$\sum_{i\in X}b_i=1.$$
answer: Proof: WLOG $\sum_X a_i<1$ and put $\Delta=\sum_{X^c}a_i-\sum_X a_i>0$. Minimality forces $a_{j+1}-a_j\ge\Delta$ whenever $j\in X$, $j+1\notin X$ (and $a_1\ge\Delta$ if $X=\{k,\dots,n\}$); then move $\Delta/2$ from $a_{j+1}$ to $a_j$ (or from $a_1$ to $a_n$), with a tiny extra shift $\varepsilon$ in the equality case.

prompt:
Let $n\ge2$ be a positive integer and $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ be real numbers such that
$$a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n=0.$$
Define the set $A$ by
$$A=\big\{(i,j)\ \big|\ 1\le i<j\le n,\ |a_i-a_j|\ge1\big\}.$$
Prove that, if $A$ is not empty, then
$$\sum_{(i,j)\in A}a_ia_j<0.$$
answer: Proof: over ordered pairs, $\sum_A a_ia_j=-\frac12\sum_{|a_i-a_j|<1}a_ia_j$. The sum over close pairs is at least $\sum_{|a_i|\ge1}a_i^2+\big(\sum_{|a_i|<1}a_i\big)^2\ge0$, and the inequality is strict when $A\neq\varnothing$.

prompt:
Let $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$ be different real numbers. Prove that
$$\sum_{1\le i\le n}\ \prod_{j\ne i}\frac{1-x_ix_j}{x_i-x_j}=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if $n$ is even;}\\[2pt]1,&\text{if $n$ is odd.}\end{cases}$$
answer: Proof: interpolate $f(t)=\prod_i(1-x_it)$ (degree $n$) at the $n+2$ nodes $x_1,\dots,x_n,1,-1$; the coefficient of $t^{n+1}$ in the Lagrange formula is $0=-G+\frac12+\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}2$, where $G$ is the given sum.

prompt:
A polynomial $P(x,y,z)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$P(x,y,z)=P(x,y,xy-z)=P(x,zx-y,z)=P(yz-x,y,z).$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$P(x,y,z)=F(x^2+y^2+z^2-xyz).$$
answer: Proof: $P(x,y,z)=P(x,y,xy-z)$ forces $P$ to be a polynomial in $x,y,z(xy-z)$, so every top-degree monomial $x^ay^bz^c$ has $a,b\ge c$; by symmetry $a=b=c$, so the top part is $\mu(xyz)^c$. Subtract $\mu(xyz-x^2-y^2-z^2)^c$ and induct on the degree.

prompt:
Let $\mathbb Z$ be the set of integers. We consider functions $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ satisfying
$$f\big(f(x+y)+y\big)=f\big(f(x)+y\big)$$
for all integers $x$ and $y$. For such a function, we say that an integer $v$ is *$f$-rare* if the set
$$X_v=\{x\in\mathbb Z:\ f(x)=v\}$$
is finite and nonempty.

(a) Prove that there exists such a function $f$ for which there is an $f$-rare integer.

(b) Prove that no such function $f$ can have more than one $f$-rare integer.
answer: (a) $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=$ the largest power of $2$ dividing $2x$ for $x\ne0$ works, with $0$ rare. (b) A rare $v$ is a fixed point (use $x=v$, $y=a-v$ and $y=b-v$ with $a,b$ the least/greatest elements of $X_v$); after translating so $v=0$, a second rare $v'$ would satisfy $f(kv')=v'$ for all $k\ge1$.

prompt:
The infinite sequence $a_0,a_1,a_2,\dots$ of (not necessarily different) integers has the following properties: $0\le a_i\le i$ for all integers $i\ge0$, and
$$\binom{k}{a_0}+\binom{k}{a_1}+\dots+\binom{k}{a_k}=2^k$$
for all integers $k\ge0$.

Prove that all integers $N\ge0$ occur in the sequence (that is, for all $N\ge0$, there exists $i\ge0$ with $a_i=N$).
answer: Proof: by induction, for every $k$ the multiset $\{a_0,\dots,a_k\}$ equals $\{0,1,\dots,\ell-1\}\cup\{0,1,\dots,k-\ell\}$ for some $\ell$ with $2\ell\le k+1$ (comparing with $\sum_i\binom{k+1}{i}=2^{k+1}$ forces $\binom{k+1}{a_{k+1}}=\binom{k+1}{\ell}$). Taking $k=2N$ shows $N$ appears among $a_0,\dots,a_{2N}$.

prompt: You are given a set of $n$ blocks, each weighing at least $1$; their total weight is $2n$. Prove that for every real number $r$ with $0\le r\le2n-2$ you can choose a subset of the blocks whose total weight is at least $r$ but at most $r+2$.
answer: Proof: sort the weights $x_1\le\dots\le x_n$; by induction the subset sums of $x_1,\dots,x_k$ have gaps at most $2$, because $x_k\le x_1+\dots+x_{k-1}+2$ (otherwise $2n>(n+1-k)(k+1)+k-1$, i.e. $n>k(n+1-k)$, which is false).

prompt:
On a flat plane in Camelot, King Arthur builds a labyrinth $\mathfrak L$ consisting of $n$ walls, each of which is an infinite straight line. No two walls are parallel, and no three walls have a common point. Merlin then paints one side of each wall entirely red and the other side entirely blue.

At the intersection of two walls there are four corners: two diagonally opposite corners where a red side and a blue side meet, one corner where two red sides meet, and one corner where two blue sides meet. At each such intersection, there is a two-way door connecting the two diagonally opposite corners at which sides of different colours meet.

After Merlin paints the walls, Morgana then places some knights in the labyrinth. The knights can walk through doors, but cannot walk through walls.

Let $k(\mathfrak L)$ be the largest number $k$ such that, no matter how Merlin paints the labyrinth $\mathfrak L$, Morgana can always place at least $k$ knights such that no two of them can ever meet. For each $n$, what are all possible values for $k(\mathfrak L)$, where $\mathfrak L$ is a labyrinth with $n$ walls?

Let $n>1$ be an integer. Suppose we are given $2n$ points in a plane such that no three of them are collinear. The points are to be labelled $A_1,A_2,\dots,A_{2n}$ in some order. We then consider the $2n$ angles $\angle A_1A_2A_3,\ \angle A_2A_3A_4,\ \dots,\ \angle A_{2n-2}A_{2n-1}A_{2n},\ \angle A_{2n-1}A_{2n}A_1,\ \angle A_{2n}A_1A_2$. We measure each angle in the way that gives the smallest positive value (i.e. between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$). Prove that there exists an ordering of the given points such that the resulting $2n$ angles can be separated into two groups with the sum of one group of angles equal to the sum of the other group.
answer: Proof: take a line $\ell$ with $n$ points on each side and let the cyclic order alternate between the sides. Rotate a line about $A_1,A_2,\dots$ in turn from $A_{i-1}A_i$ to $A_iA_{i+1}$ through the angle at $A_i$. It is never parallel to $\ell$, so the total signed rotation is $0$; group the angles by rotation direction.

prompt:
There are $60$ empty boxes $B_1,\dots,B_{60}$ in a row on a table and an unlimited supply of pebbles. Given a positive integer $n$, Alice and Bob play the following game.

In the first round, Alice takes $n$ pebbles and distributes them into the $60$ boxes as she wishes. Each subsequent round consists of two steps:

(a) Bob chooses an integer $k$ with $1\le k\le59$ and splits the boxes into the two groups $B_1,\dots,B_k$ and $B_{k+1},\dots,B_{60}$.

(b) Alice picks one of these two groups, adds one pebble to each box in that group, and removes one pebble from each box in the other group.

Bob wins if, at the end of any round, some box contains no pebbles. Find the smallest $n$ such that Alice can prevent Bob from winning.

Alice has a map of Wonderland, a country consisting of $n\ge2$ towns. For every pair of towns, there is a narrow road going from one town to the other. One day, all the roads are declared to be "one way" only. Alice has no information on the direction of the roads, but the King of Hearts has offered to help her. She is allowed to ask him a number of questions. For each question in turn, Alice chooses a pair of towns and the King of Hearts tells her the direction of the road connecting those two towns.

Alice wants to know whether there is at least one town in Wonderland with at most one outgoing road. Prove that she can always find out by asking at most $4n$ questions.
answer: Proof: build a spanning tree in which every town but one ($T$) has a known outgoing road ($n-1$ questions); ask $T$'s roads until two outgoing ones appear; then repeatedly ask about unknown pairs among the towns not yet known to have two outgoing roads (each answer eliminates one town) until at most $2$ remain, and check those directly. This takes at most $4n-7$ questions in total.

prompt:
For any two different real numbers $x$ and $y$, we define $D(x,y)$ to be the unique integer $d$ satisfying $2^d\le|x-y|<2^{d+1}$. Given a set of reals $\mathcal F$, and an element $x\in\mathcal F$, we say that the *scales* of $x$ in $\mathcal F$ are the values of $D(x,y)$ for $y\in\mathcal F$ with $x\ne y$.

Let $k$ be a given positive integer. Suppose that each member $x$ of $\mathcal F$ has at most $k$ different scales in $\mathcal F$ (note that these scales may depend on $x$). What is the maximum possible size of $\mathcal F$?

Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Circle $\Gamma$ passes through $A$, meets segments $AB$ and $AC$ again at points $D$ and $E$ respectively, and intersects segment $BC$ at $F$ and $G$ such that $F$ lies between $B$ and $G$. The tangent to circle $BDF$ at $F$ and the tangent to circle $CEG$ at $G$ meet at point $T$. Suppose that points $A$ and $T$ are distinct. Prove that line $AT$ is parallel to $BC$.
answer: Proof: tangent–chord and the cyclic quadrilateral $ADFG$ give $\angle(FT,BC)=\angle(BC,GA)$, and similarly $\angle(GT,BC)=\angle(BC,FA)$. So the reflection in the perpendicular bisector of $FG$ maps lines $GA,FA$ to $FT,GT$, hence $A$ to $T$, and $AT\parallel BC$.

prompt: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle and let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of altitudes from $A$, $B$, and $C$ to sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Denote by $\omega_B$ and $\omega_C$ the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, and let these circles be tangent to segments $DF$ and $DE$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. Let line $MN$ meet circles $\omega_B$ and $\omega_C$ again at $P\ne M$ and $Q\ne N$, respectively. Prove that $MP=NQ$.
answer: Proof: the right triangles $DMO_B$ and $DNO_C$ are similar (both angles at $D$ equal $\frac12\angle A$), so $\frac{DN}{DM}=\frac{r_C}{r_B}$; chord lengths give $MP=2r_B\sin\angle DMN$, $NQ=2r_C\sin\angle MND$, and the sine rule in $DMN$ finishes.

prompt: Let $P$ be a point inside triangle $ABC$. Let $AP$ meet $BC$ at $A_1$, let $BP$ meet $CA$ at $B_1$, and let $CP$ meet $AB$ at $C_1$. Let $A_2$ be the point such that $A_1$ is the midpoint of $PA_2$, let $B_2$ be the point such that $B_1$ is the midpoint of $PB_2$, and let $C_2$ be the point such that $C_1$ is the midpoint of $PC_2$. Prove that points $A_2$, $B_2$, and $C_2$ cannot all lie strictly inside the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.
answer: Proof: put the circumcentre at the origin with radius $1$ and $P=\alpha A+\beta B+\gamma C$ ($\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0$, sum $1$). Then $A_2=\frac{(1+\alpha)P-2\alpha A}{1-\alpha}$, and $\sum\frac{(1-\alpha)^2}{2(1+\alpha)}|A_2|^2=\sum\frac{(1-\alpha)^2}{2(1+\alpha)}$, so some $|A_2|,|B_2|,|C_2|$ is at least $1$.

prompt: Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD=DE$ and $\angle EDC\ne2\cdot\angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP=AE$ and $BP=BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD)+\operatorname{area}(ADE)=\operatorname{area}(ABD)+\operatorname{area}(ABP)$.
answer: Proof: $f(X)=[BCX]+[AXE]-[ABX]-[ABP]$ is affine, and the area condition is $f(D)=0$ with $D$ on the perpendicular bisector $\ell$ of $CE$. If $P\in CE$, a coordinate check shows $f\equiv0$ on $\ell$. If not, $f$ vanishes on $\ell$ only at the circumcentre $O$ of $CEP'$ ($P'$ the reflection of $P$ in $AB$) and $f(T)=-2[ABP]\neq0$ at the circumcentre $T$ of $CEP$. Finally, $O=D$ would force $\angle EDC=2\angle ADB$.

prompt: Let $I$ be the incentre of acute-angled triangle $ABC$. Let the incircle meet $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. Let line $EF$ intersect the circumcircle of the triangle at $P$ and $Q$, such that $F$ lies between $E$ and $P$. Prove that $\angle DPA+\angle AQD=\angle QIP$.
answer: Proof: the spiral similarity $\varphi$ taking kite $AFIE$ to kite $NBMC$ ($N,M$ the arc midpoints of $BC$) maps $P,Q$ to $P'=NP\cap BC$, $Q'=NQ\cap BC$; with $L$ the midpoint of $BC$, the points $P,Q,D,L$ are concyclic (harmonic division), and $MLPP'$, $MLQQ'$ are cyclic. An angle chase gives $\angle DPA+\angle AQD=\angle P'MQ'=\angle PIQ$.

prompt:
Let $\mathcal L$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function that assigns to each line $\ell\in\mathcal L$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any three lines $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3$ passing through $X$, the points $f(\ell_1)$, $f(\ell_2)$, $f(\ell_3)$ and $X$ lie on a circle.

Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for any line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

We say that a set $S$ of integers is *rootiful* if, for any positive integer $n$ and any $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_n\in S$, all integer roots of the polynomial $a_0+a_1x+\dots+a_nx^n$ are also in $S$. Find all rootiful sets of integers that contain all numbers of the form $2^a-2^b$ for positive integers $a$ and $b$.
answer: Only $S=\mathbb Z$. Every $n$ has a multiple $2^{\alpha+1}(2^{\varphi(t)}-1)\in S$ (with $n=2^\alpha t$, $t$ odd), and writing a multiple $N$ of $n$ in base $n$ makes $n$ a root of $a_kx^k+\dots+a_1x-N$ with digits in $S$, giving induction.

Let $\mathbb Z_{>0}$ be the set of positive integers. A positive integer constant $C$ is given. Find all functions $f:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Z_{>0}$ such that, for all positive integers $a$ and $b$ satisfying $a+b>C$,
$$a+f(b)\mid a^2+b\,f(a).$$
answer: $f(a)=ka$ for a positive integer constant $k$ (for every $C$). Show $b\mid f(b)^2$, so $f(p)=k(p)\,p$ with $k(p)\le f(1)$; some $k$ occurs for infinitely many primes $p$, and then $a+kp\mid f(a)-ka$ forces $f(a)=ka$.

prompt: Let $a$ be a positive integer. We say that a positive integer $b$ is *$a$-good* if $\binom{an}{b}-1$ is divisible by $an+1$ for all positive integers $n$ with $an\ge b$. Suppose $b$ is a positive integer such that $b$ is $a$-good, but $b+2$ is not $a$-good. Prove that $b+1$ is prime.
answer: Proof: $b$ is $a$-good iff $b$ is even and every prime $p\le b$ divides $a$. Then $b$ even with all $p\le b$ dividing $a$, while some prime $q\le b+2$ does not divide $a$; so $q=b+1$, since $b+2$ is even.

prompt: Let $H=\big\{\lfloor i\sqrt2\rfloor:\ i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\big\}=\{1,2,4,5,7,\dots\}$, and let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exists a constant $C$ such that, if $A\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ satisfies $|A|\ge C\sqrt n$, then there exist $a,b\in A$ such that $a-b\in H$. (Here $\mathbb Z_{>0}$ is the set of positive integers, and $\lfloor z\rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $z$.)
answer: Proof: $m\in H\iff\{m/\sqrt2\}>1-\frac1{\sqrt2}$. If no difference lies in $H$, then after shifting $\min A$ to $0$ the fractional parts $\{a_i/\sqrt2\}$ increase with $a_i$ and stay below $1-\frac1{\sqrt2}$; since $\{d/\sqrt2\}>\frac1{2\sqrt2\,d}$, AM–HM gives $(|A|-1)^2<(2\sqrt2-2)n$. So $C=1+\sqrt{2\sqrt2-2}$ works.

prompt: Prove that there is a constant $c>0$ and infinitely many positive integers $n$ with the following property: there are infinitely many positive integers that cannot be expressed as the sum of fewer than $cn\log(n)$ pairwise coprime $n^{\text{th}}$ powers.
answer: Proof: take primes $p\mid2^{2^{t-1}}+1$, $q\mid2^{2^t}+1$ and $n=\frac{(p-1)(q-1)}{2^t}$, $N=pq$. Then $n$-th powers are $0$ or $1$ mod $p$ and mod $q$, so sums of $j$ pairwise coprime $n$-th powers take at most $4$ residues mod $N$. Since $N>\frac12n\log_2n$, a residue class is missed when $j<\frac18n\ln n$.

prompt:
Let $a$ and $b$ be two positive integers. Prove that the integer
$$a^2+\left\lceil\frac{4a^2}b\right\rceil$$
is not a square. (Here $\lceil z\rceil$ denotes the least integer greater than or equal to $z$.)
answer: Proof by descent: a square $(a+k)^2$ gives a positive solution of $\lceil c^2/b\rceil=(c+k)k$ (with $c=2a$). For the one with least $k$, $bk<c<bk+k$, so $c=bk+r$ with $0<r<k$, and $(c',k')=(r,k-r)$ is a solution with smaller $k$.

$$\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{a_i}{\sqrt{a_1^2+\dots+a_i^2}}\le4\sqrt{kn}.$$
answer: Proof: split the indices into $k$ groups by the dyadic range $[2^{j-1},2^j]$ of $a_i$; the $i$-th term of group $j$ is at most $\frac{2^j}{2^{j-1}\sqrt i}$, so a group of size $p_j$ contributes $\le4\sqrt{p_j}$, and $\sum_j4\sqrt{p_j}\le4\sqrt{kn}$ by Cauchy-Schwarz.

prompt:
Consider any rectangular table having finitely many rows and columns, with a real number $a(r,c)$ in the cell in row $r$ and column $c$. A pair $(R,C)$, where $R$ is a set of rows and $C$ a set of columns, is called a *saddle pair* if the following two conditions are satisfied:

(ii) For each column $c'$, there is $c\in C$ such that $a(r,c)\le a(r,c')$ for all $r\in R$.

A saddle pair $(R,C)$ is called a *minimal pair* if for each saddle pair $(R',C')$ with $R'\subseteq R$ and $C'\subseteq C$, we have $R'=R$ and $C'=C$.

answer: Proof: for saddle pairs $(R_1,C_1)$, $(R_2,C_2)$ compose the 'domination' maps to get $\rho:R_1\to R_1$, $\sigma:C_1\to C_1$ with $a(\rho(r),c)\ge a(r,\sigma(c))$ and $|\rho(R_1)|\le|R_2|$; the stable images of $\rho,\sigma$ form a saddle subpair of $(R_1,C_1)$ with at most $|R_2|$ rows.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $BC=CA$, and let $D$ be a point inside side $AB$ such that $AD<DB$. answer: Proof: orient each bridge from $m$ to $n\equiv m^2+1$; each island has at most one outgoing arrow, and if $p>3$ divides some $x^2-x+1$ then the islands $x$ and $p+1-x$ have none, so there are at most $p-2$ bridges; infinitely many such $p$ exist by a Euclid-type argument.

answer: Proof: prove the stronger statement that $a_i$ divides neither $a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}$ nor $a_{i-1}-a_{i+1}$, by induction: insert the maximum into a good ordering of the rest; if all $n$ positions failed, some element would be blamed twice, which contradicts the ordering of the smaller set.

prompt: Let $n$ be an integer, and let $A$ be a subset of $\{0,1,2,3,\dots,5^n\}$ consisting of $4n+2$ numbers. Prove that there exist $a,b,c\in A$ such that $a<b<c$ and $c+2a>3b$.
answer: Proof: take $c=\max A$; if every consecutive pair $x_i<x_{i+1}$ failed, then $c-x_i\ge\frac32(c-x_{i+1})$, so $c-x_0\ge(3/2)^{4n}=(81/16)^n>5^n$, impossible.

answer: Proof: with $s_k=a_1+\dots+a_k$, each term satisfies $\frac{a_k}{1-a_k}s_{k-1}^2<\frac{s_k^3-s_{k-1}^3}3$; the right sides telescope to $\frac13$.

answer: The largest non-$n$-colourful number is $n^2-n-1$; every $m\ge n(n-1)$ is $n$-colourful.

prompt:
The kingdom of Anisotropy consists of $n$ cities. For every two cities there exists exactly one direct one-way road between them. We say that a *path from $X$ to $Y$* is a sequence of roads such that one can move from $X$ to $Y$ along this sequence without returning to an already visited city. A collection of paths is called *diverse* if no road belongs to two or more paths in the collection.

Let $A$ and $B$ be two distinct cities in Anisotropy. Let $N_{AB}$ denote the maximal number of paths in a diverse collection of paths from $A$ to $B$. Similarly, let $N_{BA}$ denote the maximal number of paths in a diverse collection of paths from $B$ to $A$. Prove that the equality $N_{AB}=N_{BA}$ holds if and only if the number of roads going out from $A$ is the same as the number of roads going out from $B$.
answer: Proof: in fact $N_{BA}-N_{AB}=b-a$ (out-degrees); by Menger's theorem compare minimum cuts: moving $A$ and $B$ across a cut changes its size by exactly $b-a$.

prompt:
Let $n$ and $k$ be two integers with $n>k\ge1$. There are $2n+1$ students standing in a circle. Each student $S$ has $2k$ *neighbours* — namely, the $k$ students closest to $S$ on the right, and the $k$ students closest to $S$ on the left.

Suppose that $n+1$ of the students are girls, and the other $n$ are boys. Prove that there is a girl with at least $k$ girls among her neighbours.
answer: Proof: with $a_i\in\{0,1\}$ (girl $=1$) set $b_i=a_i+a_{i-k-1}-1$; every $2n+1$ consecutive $b_i$ sum to $1$, and a gas-station style argument finds $i$ with $b_i=1$ and $b_{i+1}+\dots+b_{i+k}\ge0$, which is exactly such a girl.

prompt:
A hunter and an invisible rabbit play a game on an infinite square grid. First the hunter fixes a colouring of the cells with finitely many colours. The rabbit then secretly chooses a cell to start in. Every minute, the rabbit reports the colour of its current cell to the hunter, and then secretly moves to an adjacent cell that it has not visited before (two cells are adjacent if they share a side). The hunter wins if after some finite time either

- the rabbit cannot move; or
- the hunter can determine the cell in which the rabbit started.

Decide whether there exists a winning strategy for the hunter.
answer: Yes. Combine colourings by $x\bmod3$, $y\bmod3$ (to track every move) with three colourings marking columns, rows and diagonals $x+y=$ const at pairwise distinct gaps; two of $x,y,x+y$ must be unbounded, which pins down the start.

prompt:
Consider a checkered $3m\times3m$ square, where $m$ is an integer greater than $1$. A frog sits on the lower left corner cell $S$ and wants to get to the upper right corner cell $F$. The frog can hop from any cell to either the next cell to the right or the next cell upwards.

Some cells can be *sticky*, and the frog gets trapped once it hops on such a cell. A set $X$ of cells is called *blocking* if the frog cannot reach $F$ from $S$ when all the cells of $X$ are sticky. A blocking set is *minimal* if it does not contain a smaller blocking set.

(a) Prove that there exists a minimal blocking set containing at least $3m^2-3m$ cells.

(b) Prove that every minimal blocking set contains at most $3m^2$ cells.

*Note.* An example of a minimal blocking set for $m=2$ is shown in the picture. Cells of the set $X$ are marked by letters $x$.
answer: (a) A construction in vertical stripes of width $3$ with $3m^2-2m+2\ge3m^2-3m$ cells. (b) Colour cells reachable from $S$ red and cells from which $F$ is reachable blue; minimality gives $G\le R+1$ and $G\le B+1$ for the $G$ sticky cells, so $9m^2\ge3G-2$.

Prove that the lines $CD$, $AQ$, and $BR$ are concurrent.
answer: Proof: angle chasing shows $ABCR$ is cyclic; with $X=AQ\cap CD$, also $CQRX$ is cyclic, and then $\angle XRC=\angle BRC$-type equalities force $B,R,X$ collinear.

prompt:

Assume that $\mathcal F$ is a set consisting of $n^2$ quadrilaterals such that all their vertices lie in $S$, and each point in $S$ is a vertex of exactly one of the quadrilaterals in $\mathcal F$.

Determine the largest possible sum of areas of all $n^2$ quadrilaterals in $\mathcal F$.
answer: $\frac13n^2(2n+1)(2n-1)$, attained by the $n^2$ squares centred at the centre of the grid; the bound comes from $[P]\le\frac12\sum OA_i^2$ for every polygon.

prompt: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle $\Omega$. Let the tangent to $\Omega$ at $D$ intersect the rays $BA$ and $BC$ at points $E$ and $F$, respectively. A point $T$ is chosen inside the triangle $ABC$ so that $TE\parallel CD$ and $TF\parallel AD$. Let $K\ne D$ be a point on the segment $DF$ such that $TD=TK$. Prove that the lines $AC$, $DT$ and $BK$ intersect at one point.
answer: Proof: with $P=TE\cap AC$, $Q=TF\cap AC$, the circles $APDE$ and $CQDF$ are tangent at $D$ and $DT$ is their common tangent; then $TK\parallel BD$, $T,P,Q,D,K$ are concyclic and $PK\parallel BC$, so triangles $TPK$ and $DCB$ are homothetic and $TD,PC,KB$ concur.

prompt:
Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral whose sides have pairwise different lengths. Let $O$ be the circumcentre of $ABCD$. The internal angle bisectors of $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ADC$ meet $AC$ at $B_1$ and $D_1$, respectively. Let $O_B$ be the centre of the circle which passes through $B$ and is tangent to $AC$ at $D_1$. Similarly, let $O_D$ be the centre of the circle which passes through $D$ and is tangent to $AC$ at $B_1$.

Assume that $BD_1\parallel DB_1$. Prove that $O$ lies on the line $O_BO_D$.
answer: Proof: the radical axis of $\Omega$ and circle $O_D$ passes through $D$ and through $L_B$, where the tangent to $\Omega$ at $B$ meets $AC$ (since $L_BB=L_BB_1$); so it suffices that $BL_D\parallel DL_B$, which a computation on line $AC$ shows is equivalent to $a^2b^2(c^2-d^2)=c^2d^2(a^2-b^2)$, the same condition as $BD_1\parallel DB_1$.

prompt: Determine all integers $n\ge3$ satisfying the following property: every convex $n$-gon whose sides all have length $1$ contains an equilateral triangle of side length $1$. (Every polygon is assumed to contain its boundary.)
answer: All odd $n\ge3$. (For even $n$, a thin symmetric polygon cut from a huge regular polygon fits in a narrow strip; for odd $n$, use the longest diagonal $A_0A_\ell$ with $\ell\ge\frac{n+1}2$.)

prompt: Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of a triangle $ABC$, and let $\Omega_A$ be its excircle which is tangent to the segment $BC$. The tangent line at $P$ to the circumcircle of the triangle $APX$ intersects the tangent line at $Q$ to the circumcircle of the triangle $AQY$ at a point $R$. Prove that $AR\perp BC$.
answer: Proof: let $R'$ be the point on the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ lying on the tangent to $\Omega_A$ parallel to $BC$ (opposite to $BC$); Brianchon's theorem and two cyclic quadrilaterals show $PR'$ is tangent to $(APX)$, and likewise $QR'$ to $(AQY)$, so $R=R'$.

prompt:
Determine all integers $n\ge1$ for which there exists a pair of positive integers $(a,b)$ such that no cube of a prime divides $a^2+b+3$ and

Find all positive integers $n$ with the following property: the $k$ positive divisors of $n$ have a permutation $(d_1,d_2,\dots,d_k)$ such that for every $i=1,2,\dots,k$, the number $d_1+\dots+d_i$ is a perfect square.

Alice is given a rational number $r>1$ and a line with two points $B\ne R$, where point $R$ contains a red bead and point $B$ contains a blue bead. Alice plays a solitaire game by performing a sequence of moves. In every move, she chooses a (not necessarily positive) integer $k$, and a bead to move. If that bead is placed at point $X$, and the other bead is placed at $Y$, then Alice moves the chosen bead to point $X'$ with $\overrightarrow{YX'}=r^k\,\overrightarrow{YX}$.

Alice's goal is to move the red bead to the point $B$. Find all rational numbers $r>1$ such that Alice can reach her goal in at most $2021$ moves.

Prove that there are only finitely many quadruples $(a,b,c,n)$ of positive integers such that
$$n!=a^{n-1}+b^{n-1}+c^{n-1}.$$
answer: Proof: there are no solutions with $n>100$: AM–GM gives $a,b,c<\frac{n-1}2$; odd $n$ fails by a mod $4$ / $2$-adic argument; for even $n$ either all pairwise sums are powers of $2$ (quickly impossible) or an odd prime $p\mid a+b$ and LTE with Legendre's formula give a contradiction.

prompt: Determine all integers $n\ge2$ with the following property: every $n$ pairwise distinct integers whose sum is not divisible by $n$ can be arranged in some order $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ so that $n$ divides $1\cdot a_1+2\cdot a_2+\dots+n\cdot a_n$.
answer: All odd $n$ and all powers of $2$.

prompt: Let $a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots$ be an infinite sequence of positive integers such that $a_{n+2m}$ divides $a_n+a_{n+m}$ for all positive integers $n$ and $m$. Prove that this sequence is eventually periodic, i.e. there exist positive integers $N$ and $d$ such that $a_n=a_{n+d}$ for all $n>N$.
answer: Proof: the sequence is bounded (a new record $k=a_n$ would force $a_{n-s}+a_{n-2s}=k$ and then $k\le2\max(a_1,\dots,a_6)$); after truncation every value recurs, the indices of terms divisible by any fixed $d$ form an arithmetic progression with odd difference, and the product of these differences is a period.

prompt: For a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients let $P^1(x)=P(x)$ and $P^{k+1}(x)=P(P^k(x))$ for $k\ge1$. Find all positive integers $n$ for which there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for every integer $m\ge1$, the numbers $P^m(1),\dots,P^m(n)$ leave exactly $\lceil n/2^m\rceil$ distinct remainders when divided by $n$.
answer: All powers of $2$ and all primes.

prompt:
Let $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ be a sequence of positive real numbers with the property that
$$(a_{n+1})^2+a_na_{n+2}\le a_n+a_{n+2}$$
for all positive integers $n$. Show that $a_{2022}\le 1$.
answer: Proof: rewrite the condition as $a_{n+1}^2-1\le(1-a_n)(a_{n+2}-1)$; this shows that no two consecutive terms $a_{n+1},a_{n+2}$ can both exceed $1$, and then $a_{2022}>1$ gives $0<a_{2022}^2-1\le(1-a_{2021})(a_{2023}-1)\le0$.

prompt: Let $k\ge2$ be an integer. Find the smallest integer $n\ge k+1$ with the property that there exists a set of $n$ distinct real numbers such that each of its elements can be written as a sum of $k$ other distinct elements of the set.

Let $n\ge3$ be an integer, and let $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$ be real numbers in the interval $[0,1]$. Let $s=x_1+x_2+\dots+x_n$, and assume that $s\ge3$. Prove that there exist integers $i$ and $j$ with $1\le i<j\le n$ such that
$$2^{j-i}x_ix_j>2^{s-3}.$$
answer: Proof: take $a<b$ maximising $2^{b-a}x_ax_b$; maximality gives the geometric bounds $x_i\le2^{i-a}x_a$ ($i<b$) and $x_j\le2^{b-j}x_b$ ($j>a$). With $x_a=2^{-\alpha}$, $x_b=2^{-\beta}$, $u=\lfloor\alpha\rfloor$, $v=\lfloor\beta\rfloor$, summing these bounds and using $2^\theta\le1+\theta$ on $[0,1]$ gives $s<b-a-\alpha-\beta+3$.

prompt: Find all positive integers $n\ge2$ for which there exist $n$ real numbers $a_1<\dots<a_n$ and a real number $r>0$ such that the $\frac12n(n-1)$ differences $a_j-a_i$ for $1\le i<j\le n$ are equal, in some order, to the numbers $r^1,r^2,\dots,r^{\frac12n(n-1)}$.
answer: $n\in\{2,3,4\}$. (Constructions: $r=2$; the golden ratio with $(0,r,r+r^2)$; the real root of $r^3=r+1$ with $(0,r,r+r^2,r+r^2+r^3)$. For $n\ge5$, writing $a_n-a_1=r^b$ as $(a_n-a_i)+(a_i-a_1)$ forces $r^b=r^{b-i}+r^{\alpha_i}$ with tightly spaced $\alpha_i$, leading to $r^{n-1}=r+1$ and $r^3=r+1$, so $n=4$.)

prompt:
Let $\mathbb R$ be the set of real numbers. We denote by $\mathcal F$ the set of all functions $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$f(x+f(y))=f(x)+f(y)$$
for every $x,y\in\mathbb R$. Find all rational numbers $q$ such that for every function $f\in\mathcal F$, there exists some $z\in\mathbb R$ satisfying $f(z)=qz$.
answer: Exactly $q=\frac{n+1}{n}$ with $n$ a nonzero integer. (From $f(x+f(0))=f(x)+f(0)$ we get $f(nf(0))=(n+1)f(0)$, so $z=nf(0)$ works; for other $q$, a function $f(x)=g(\{x\})+\lfloor x\rfloor$ with integer-valued $g$ avoids $f(z)=qz$.)

prompt: For a positive integer $n$ we denote by $s(n)$ the sum of the digits of $n$. Let $P(x)=x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots+a_1x+a_0$ be a polynomial, where $n\ge2$ and $a_i$ is a positive integer for all $0\le i\le n-1$. Could it be the case that, for all positive integers $k$, $s(k)$ and $s(P(k))$ have the same parity?
answer: No. Choose $X\equiv1\pmod{100}$ and $m$ so that $a_{n-1}X^{n-1}$ has $m+1$ digits with leading digit $9$ and all other terms are short; then $s(P(10^{m+1}X))-s(P(10^mX))=9$ (one carry $9+1$), while $s(10^{m+1}X)=s(10^mX)$.

prompt:
For a positive integer $n$, an *$n$-sequence* is a sequence $(a_0,\dots,a_n)$ of non-negative integers satisfying the following condition: if $i$ and $j$ are non-negative integers with $i+j\le n$, then $a_i+a_j\le n$ and $a_{a_i+a_j}=a_{i+j}$.

Let $f(n)$ be the number of $n$-sequences. Prove that there exist positive real numbers $c_1$, $c_2$ and $\lambda$ such that
$$c_1\lambda^n<f(n)<c_2\lambda^n$$
for all positive integers $n$.
answer: Proof with $\lambda=3^{1/6}$: apart from the identity, an $n$-sequence is eventually periodic with offset $r$ and period $d$, with $a_i\equiv i$ (or $i+\frac d2$) mod $d$; with $k=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, those with a value $>k$ are determined by $(r,d)$, the others by a period with entries in $[r,k]$. Counting periods gives both bounds ($3^{\lfloor(k+1)/3\rfloor}$ periodic examples below; $\prod m_i\le3^{x/3}\rho^{|x-3d|}$ above).

- The lumberjack then chooses four different squares on the board. Each tree of positive height on those squares then becomes one unit shorter.

We say that a tree is *majestic* if its height is at least $10^6$. Determine the largest number $K$ such that the gardener can ensure there are eventually $K$ majestic trees on the board, no matter how the lumberjack plays.

Let $n>3$ be a positive integer. Suppose that $n$ children are arranged in a circle, and $n$ coins are distributed between them (some children may have no coins). At every step, a child with at least $2$ coins may give $1$ coin to each of their immediate neighbours on the right and left. Determine all initial distributions of coins from which it is possible that, after a finite number of steps, each child has exactly one coin.
answer: Number the children $1,\dots,n$ around the circle and let child $i$ start with $c_i$ coins: exactly the distributions with $\sum_{i=1}^n ic_i\equiv\frac{n(n+1)}2\pmod n$. ($\sum ic_i$ mod $n$ is invariant; conversely solve $Lu=\mathbf 1-c$ for a firing vector $u\ge0$, and a 'least action' argument shows greedy play stops at all ones.)

prompt:
Let $m,n\ge2$ be integers, let $X$ be a set with $n$ elements, and let $X_1,X_2,\dots,X_m$ be pairwise distinct non-empty, not necessarily disjoint subsets of $X$. A function $f:X\to\{1,2,\dots,n+1\}$ is called *nice* if there exists an index $k$ such that

answer: Proof: for each of the $n^n$ functions $f:X\to\{1,\dots,n\}$, pick a set $X_l$ maximising $f(X_l)$ and add $1$ on $X_l$. The new function $f^+$ is nice with unique maximiser $X_l$ (no $X_j$ contains $X_l$ properly), and $f$ can be recovered from $f^+$, so this is an injection into the nice functions.

prompt: Let $n$ be a positive integer. We start with $n$ piles of pebbles, each initially containing a single pebble. One can perform moves of the following form: choose two piles, take an equal number of pebbles from each pile and form a new pile out of these pebbles. For each positive integer $n$, find the smallest number of non-empty piles that one can obtain by performing a finite sequence of moves of this form.
answer: $1$ if $n$ is a power of $2$, and $2$ otherwise. (Odd divisors of all piles are preserved backwards in time, so a single pile of $n$ needs $n$ to have no odd divisor $>1$; two piles are always reachable.)

prompt:

The lines through $P$ parallel to $AC$ and $AB$ meet $BC$ at $D$ and $E$, respectively. Points $X\ne A$ and $Y\ne A$ lie on the circles $ABD$ and $ACE$, respectively, such that $DA=DX$ and $EA=EY$.

Thales gives $FD\cdot FB=FE\cdot FC$, so the radical axis of circles $ABD$, $ACE$ is the altitude $AF\ni A'$, whence $A'B\cdot A'X=A'C\cdot A'Y$.

prompt: In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, point $H$ is the foot of the altitude from $A$. answer: Proof: the fixed point is $K$, the intersection of the reflections of $BC$ in $AB$ and $AC$. prompt: Let $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ be two triangles having the same circumcircle $\omega$, and the same orthocentre $H$. Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of the triangle determined by the lines $AA'$, $BB'$ and $CC'$. Prove that $H$, the centre of $\omega$, and the centre of $\Omega$ are collinear.
answer: Proof: both triangles have the same centroid and the same nine-point circle $\rho$ (centre on $OH$). Show $\omega$, $\Omega$, $\rho$ are coaxial: with $D=BB'\cap CC'$, $S=BC'\cap B'C$ and $N$ the midpoint of $SD$, Brocard's theorem gives $ND^2=\operatorname{pow}_\omega(N)$, an angle chase (using $MM'\parallel AA'$) shows $SD$ is tangent to $\Omega$ and to circle $DMM'$ at $D$, and the Newton–Gauss line gives $ND^2=NM\cdot NM'=\operatorname{pow}_\rho(N)$.

prompt:
Let $AA'BCC'B'$ be a convex cyclic hexagon such that $AC$ is tangent to the incircle of the triangle $A'B'C'$, and $A'C'$ is tangent to the incircle of the triangle $ABC$. Let the lines $AB$ and $A'B'$ meet at $X$ and let the lines $BC$ and $B'C'$ meet at $Y$.

Prove that if $XBYB'$ is a convex quadrilateral, then it has an incircle.
answer: Proof: with $I,I'$ the incentres, $B,I,I',B'$ are concyclic; Poncelet-type arguments produce $Z$ on the circle with $I$ the incentre of $ZA'C'$, and radical-axis/Monge arguments show that the external homothety centre $T$ of the two incircles lies on $BB'$. Then Monge for the incircle of $A'B'C'$, the circle tangent to $A'B'$, $B'C'$, $AB$, and the incircle of $ABC$ shows that this circle is also tangent to $BC$.

prompt:
A number is called *Norwegian* if it has three distinct positive divisors whose sum is equal to $2022$. Determine the smallest Norwegian number.

(Note: The total number of positive divisors of a Norwegian number is allowed to be larger than $3$.)

Find all positive integers $n>2$ such that
$$n!\ \Big|\ \prod_{\substack{p<q\le n\\ p,q\ \text{primes}}}(p+q).$$

Let $a>1$ be a positive integer, and let $d>1$ be a positive integer coprime to $a$. Let $x_1=1$ and, for $k\ge1$, define
$$x_{k+1}=\begin{cases}x_k+d&\text{if }a\text{ doesn't divide }x_k,\\ x_k/a&\text{if }a\text{ divides }x_k.\end{cases}$$
Find the greatest positive integer $n$ for which there exists an index $k$ such that $x_k$ is divisible by $a^n$.
answer: The $n$ with $d<a^n<ad$, i.e. the largest $n$ with $a^{n-1}<d$. (All terms are $<ad$; and the first term $\equiv a^n\pmod d$, which comes right after a division and is $<d$, climbs by steps of $d$ exactly to $a^n$.)

prompt:
For each $1\le i\le9$ and $T\in\mathbb N$, define $d_i(T)$ to be the total number of times the digit $i$ appears when all the multiples of $1829$ between $1$ and $T$ inclusive are written out in base $10$.

Show that there are infinitely many $T\in\mathbb N$ such that there are precisely two distinct values among $d_1(T),d_2(T),\dots,d_9(T)$.
answer: Proof: take $k$ with $1829\mid10^k-1$. Rotating the digits of a $k$-digit string multiplies it by $10$ mod $10^k-1$, so the multiples of $1829$ below $10^k$ are closed under rotation; thus $d_i(10^k-1)=k\cdot\#\{\text{multiples with leading digit }i\}\in\{kq,k(q+1)\}$. Then $T=10^k-1$ or $T=10^k-2$ works.

prompt:
Let $Q$ be a set of prime numbers, not necessarily finite. For a positive integer $n$ consider its prime factorisation; define $p(n)$ to be the sum of all the exponents and $q(n)$ to be the sum of the exponents corresponding only to primes in $Q$. A positive integer $n$ is called *special* if $p(n)+p(n+1)$ and $q(n)+q(n+1)$ are both even integers. Prove that there is a constant $c>0$ independent of the set $Q$ such that for any positive integer $N>100$, the number of special integers in $[1,N]$ is at least $cN$.

(For example, if $Q=\{3,7\}$, then $p(42)=3$, $q(42)=2$, $p(63)=3$, $q(63)=3$, $p(2022)=3$, $q(2022)=1$.)
answer: Proof with $c=\frac1{2000}$: among any five numbers two have the same parities of $(p,q)$ (*friends*); friendship is preserved by dividing both by a common divisor. In $\{72k,72k+6,72k+8,72k+9,72k+12\}$ every difference divides both numbers, so some quotient pair $(m,m+1)$ are friends; this gives a special number in a 10-element set $S_k\subseteq[1,100k]$.

prompt: Prove that $5^n-3^n$ is not divisible by $2^n+65$ for any positive integer $n$.
answer: Proof: $n$ must be odd and $\ge3$ (else $3\mid2^n+65$ or $n=1$ fails), so $m=2^n+65\equiv1\pmod 8$, $m\equiv1\pmod3$, $m\equiv\pm2\pmod5$. Jacobi symbols: $\left(\frac5m\right)=\left(\frac m5\right)=-1$ but $\left(\frac3m\right)=\left(\frac m3\right)=1$, while $5^n\equiv3^n\pmod m$ with $n$ odd would force $\left(\frac5m\right)=\left(\frac3m\right)$.

prompt:

The total capacity of all the bowls is $100$ kilograms. Professor Oak distributes $100$ kilograms of food in such a way that each Pokémon receives a non-negative integer number of kilograms of food (which may be larger than the capacity of their bowl). The *dissatisfaction level* of a Pokémon who received $N$ kilograms of food and whose bowl has a capacity of $C$ kilograms is equal to $|N-C|$.

Find the smallest real number $D$ such that, regardless of the capacities of the bowls, Professor Oak can distribute the food in a way that the sum of the dissatisfaction levels over all the $100$ Pokémon is at most $D$.

Let $\mathbb R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a function such that
$$f(x+y)f(x-y)\ge f(x)^2-f(y)^2$$
for every $x,y\in\mathbb R$. Assume that the inequality is strict for some $x_0,y_0\in\mathbb R$.

Prove that $f(x)\ge0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R$ or $f(x)\le0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R$.
answer: Put $s=x+y$, $t=x-y$ and add the inequality for $(s,t)$ and $(s,-t)$: $f(s)\big(f(t)+f(-t)\big)\ge0$ for all $s,t$, strictly for $t_0=x_0-y_0$, so every $f(s)$ has the sign of $f(t_0)+f(-t_0)\ne0$ (or is $0$).

prompt:
Let $\mathbb R_{>0}$ be the set of positive real numbers. Determine all functions $f:\mathbb R_{>0}\to\mathbb R_{>0}$ such that
$$x\big(f(x)+f(y)\big)\ge\big(f(f(x))+y\big)f(y)$$
for every $x,y\in\mathbb R_{>0}$.
answer: $f(x)=\frac{c}{x}$ for any constant $c>0$ (show $f(f(y))=y$ by iterating, then $xf(x)\ge yf(y)$ for all $x,y$).

for every $k=1,2,\dots,N$.
answer: Round $\sqrt j$ to the nearest integer: for $N=m(m+1)$ the rounded values form two copies of the multiset $\{1^{\times1},2^{\times2},\dots,m^{\times m}\}$, which can be arranged in three rows with every column summing to $2m+1$; for general $N$ insert the extra $t\le2m+1$ numbers just above $\lfloor 4N/9\rfloor$. The error is below $8.5$.
Exactly the pairs with $3\mid mn$. (Colour cell $(i,j)$ by $i+j \bmod 3$: every move flips one coin of each colour.)

He wishes to cut the strip into several pieces, where each piece consists of a number of consecutive unit squares, and then translate (without rotating or flipping) the pieces to obtain an $n\times n$ square satisfying the following property: if the unit square in the $i$-th row and $j$-th column is labelled with $a_{ij}$, then $a_{ij}-(i+j-1)$ is divisible by $n$.

Determine the smallest number of pieces Paul needs to make in order to accomplish this.

Elisa has $2023$ treasure chests, all of which are unlocked and empty at first. Each day, Elisa adds a new gem to one of the unlocked chests of her choice, and afterwards, a fairy acts according to the following rules:
- if more than one chests are unlocked, it locks one of them, or
- if there is only one unlocked chest, it unlocks all the chests.

Given that this process goes on forever, prove that there is a constant $C$ with the following property: Elisa can ensure that the difference between the numbers of gems in any two chests never exceeds $C$, regardless of how the fairy chooses the chests to lock.
answer: $C=2022$ works if Elisa always fills the emptiest unlocked chest: the sorted gem counts are always majorised by the explicit sequence $b^t_i=i-1012+\#\{s\le t: s\equiv i \pmod{2023}\}$, whose spread is at most $2022$.

prompt:
Let $N$ be a positive integer, and consider an $N\times N$ grid. A *right-down path* is a sequence of grid cells such that each cell is either one cell to the right of or one cell below the previous cell in the sequence. A *right-up path* is a sequence of grid cells such that each cell is either one cell to the right of or one cell above the previous cell in the sequence.

Prove that the cells of the $N\times N$ grid cannot be partitioned into less than $N$ right-down or right-up paths. For example, the following partition of the $5\times5$ grid uses $5$ paths.
answer: Cut each cell along a diagonal so that consecutive cells of a path form parallelograms of two half-cells; $k$ paths leave $2k$ uncovered half-cells. Treat the diagonals as mirrors and shine lasers in from the $4N$ boundary edges: a counting of the $2N$ beams shows they pass through at least $2N$ uncovered half-cells, so $k\ge N$.

prompt:
